cards.title: Disjoint-union closure of tractable forbidden patterns
cards.formal: For every pair of fixed nonempty finite simple graphs H₁,H₂, is the following implication true? If Independent Set parameterized by the requested set size k is fixed-parameter tractable on H₁-free graphs and is fixed-parameter tractable on H₂-free graphs, then it is fixed-parameter tractable on (H₁⊔H₂)-free graphs. Here exclusion is as an induced subgraph, ⊔ is disjoint union of the forbidden patterns, and fixed-parameter tractability has the deterministic meaning defined below. The two forbidden graphs may themselves be disconnected and may be isomorphic.
cards.why: A closure theorem would reduce the classification of parameterized Independent Set with one forbidden induced pattern to its connected components. It would organize many currently separate tractability results through one general structural principle.
cards.status_note: Read the original conjecture, induced-exclusion definition and parameter convention, the expanded journal manuscript’s conclusion, and the later ISAAC paper’s individual-pattern results and randomness qualification. Searched subsequent work without finding a resolution of the full closure implication. This is a source-grounded open status, not an exhaustive absence proof. No independent proof verification.

sentences: Independent Set asks whether a graph contains k pairwise nonadjacent vertices.
Suppose the problem is fixed-parameter tractable when either one of two fixed induced patterns is forbidden.
The conjecture asks whether tractability persists when only their disjoint union is forbidden.
This is already known when the forbidden components are cliques, and the 2020 journal manuscript retains the general conjecture.
The problem concerns the forbidden pattern, not whether the input graph itself is disconnected.

references.title: Parameterized Complexity of Independent Set in H-Free Graphs
references.authors: Bonnet, Édouard; Bousquet, Nicolas; Charbit, Pierre; Thomassé, Stéphan; Watrigant, Rémi

cards.definitions: For a fixed graph H, an input to Independent Set on H-free graphs is a finite simple undirected graph G on n labeled vertices, encoded by its adjacency matrix, and a binary integer k with 0≤k≤n, under the promise that no subset of V(G) induces a graph isomorphic to H. The answer is YES exactly when there is a set S⊆V(G) with |S|≥k and no edge between distinct members of S. Only k is the parameter; H is fixed in the definition of the restricted problem and is not supplied as a variable-size input. Call H tractable if there exist a deterministic algorithm A_H, a total computable function f_H:ℕ→ℕ and a constant c_H≥0 such that A_H correctly decides every promised input in at most f_H(k)(n+1)^{c_H} bit operations. The algorithm is uniform over n,k and its guarantees are worst-case and exact. Behavior outside the H-free promise is unrestricted. Constants, algorithms and computable functions may depend on H, while c_H cannot depend on k or n. For H₁⊔H₂ take disjoint copies of their vertex sets, preserve the edges within each copy, and put no edges between copies. Thus a graph contains an induced H₁⊔H₂ precisely when it has disjoint induced copies of H₁ and H₂ with no cross-edge between them. Excluding this one disconnected pattern is weaker than simultaneously excluding both H₁ and H₂. The conjecture says that the set of tractable forbidden patterns is closed under ⊔. Its quantifier is over existence of algorithms for each fixed pair; it does not additionally demand one effective transformation that constructs an algorithm from descriptions of H₁,H₂ or from the two assumed algorithms. Input graphs G are not promised to be disconnected. Weighted Independent Set and randomized fixed-parameter algorithms define different variants; this card uses the source’s unqualified deterministic FPT convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed H₁,H₂ satisfying the two tractability premises there exist an algorithm A, a computable f and a constant c, all allowed to depend on that pair, deciding the (H₁⊔H₂)-free problem in f(k)(n+1)^c time; or refute this universal implication. A refutation must establish both premises and failure of the conclusion for its pair. A W[1]-hardness proof for the conclusion is only a conditional refutation unless the relevant FPT-versus-W[1] separation is assumed explicitly. A result for the intersection of the two graph classes or for disjoint input components does not settle this statement.

context_blocks.title: Combining forbidden patterns changes the input class
context_blocks.text: Every H₁-free or H₂-free input is automatically (H₁⊔H₂)-free, but the latter class can also contain both patterns. The conjecture asks whether this enlargement preserves parameterized tractability. It is not the elementary decomposition of Independent Set across disconnected input components.

context_blocks.title: The source proves an important special case
context_blocks.text: When the forbidden graph is a disjoint union of cliques, the paper gives an FPT algorithm. The concluding conjecture asks whether the same closure principle holds for all tractable forbidden patterns, not only clique components.

context_blocks.title: The expanded paper retains the conjecture
context_blocks.text: The author-hosted Algorithmica manuscript repeats the disjoint-union implication in its conclusion. It also distinguishes this question from another proposed closure operation, adding false twins, which the paper shows does not preserve the hoped-for tractability classification under the usual complexity separation.

context_blocks.title: Subsequent special-case progress has a randomness qualification
context_blocks.text: The ISAAC 2019 follow-up provides additional tractable forbidden patterns and randomized FPT algorithms for dart- and cricket-free graphs. These results concern individual patterns and do not prove the general disjoint-union implication. In particular, a randomized result is not silently substituted for the deterministic premises here.

cards.context:
Every H₁-free or H₂-free input is automatically (H₁⊔H₂)-free, but the latter class can also contain both patterns. The conjecture asks whether this enlargement preserves parameterized tractability. It is not the elementary decomposition of Independent Set across disconnected input components.

When the forbidden graph is a disjoint union of cliques, the paper gives an FPT algorithm. The concluding conjecture asks whether the same closure principle holds for all tractable forbidden patterns, not only clique components.

The author-hosted Algorithmica manuscript repeats the disjoint-union implication in its conclusion. It also distinguishes this question from another proposed closure operation, adding false twins, which the paper shows does not preserve the hoped-for tractability classification under the usual complexity separation.

The ISAAC 2019 follow-up provides additional tractable forbidden patterns and randomized FPT algorithms for dart- and cricket-free graphs. These results concern individual patterns and do not prove the general disjoint-union implication. In particular, a randomized result is not silently substituted for the deterministic premises here.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
